Characterization of Detonation Wave Propagation in a Rotating Detonation Rocket Engine using Direct High-Speed Imaging
Automated image processing method to quantify rotating detonation wave behavior
top_cited_works.abstract: An image processing technique is developed to automatically determine both average and instantaneous detonation wave properties within a rotating detonation rocket engine (RDRE) using high-speed imaging. This method entails segmenting the imaged RDRE annulus into 200 azimuthal bins and tracking integrated pixel intensity in each bin. By combining individual pixel intensity temporal histories across the azimuthal bins, this provides what is termed a detonation surface that visualizes the propagation of the individual detonation fronts azimuthally around the annulus. Average detonation modal properties including wave speed Ūwv, operational frequency fdet, and the number of waves m are determined automatically through a two-dimensional Fourier analysis of the detonation surface data. Also, instantaneous wave speeds Uwv for each individual detonation are determined by taking the numerical derivative of each waves’ angular position temporal history from the detonation surface. This provides useful insight into wave-to-wave variability for an operating condition, as well as denoting modal transitions and mode stability. On the Determination of Rotating Detonation Engine Wave Modes Using Limited Point Measurements
recent_works.abstract: A method to determine the average modal parameters in a rotating detonation engine (RDE) for a limited set of point measurements using the 2D discrete Fourier Transform (fast Fourier transform) is described, and a new sensor placement inspired by the field of compressed sensing is identified based on success of this method in predicting the wave count m and operating frequency f_det in a suite of synthetic case studies of steady-state RDE operation. The performance of this new, “prime” sensor placement is compared to the NASA SP-194 [1] and equidistant (uniform) sensor placements, which are both in use today for determining RDE modes using point measurements. For the synthetic case studies tested, the newly proposed sensor placement is demonstrated to outperform both the SP-194 and equidistant placements for each deployed sensor count between M = 2 and 5. The performance of the proposed prime sensor placement is comparable to the SP-194 recommendations for (co-)rotating wave modes, both with and without concern for the wave direction, and outperforms the SP-194 placement strategy for more complex wave modes. recent_works.title: A Steam Engine for the Space Age: Thermodynamic Analysis of a Detonation Thruster With Water Electrolysis Propellant Generation
recent_works.abstract: A thermodynamic model of a water electrolysis system is developed and integrated into a thermodynamic system model of a detonative combustion engine to enable the analysis of theoretical small-spacecraft detonation propulsion systems using water electrolysis for propellant generation. Due to the additional time required to generate propellants via electrolysis, these thrusters lend themselves well to infrequent, impulsive firings rather than sustained burns. Performance characteristics including specific impulse, energy efficiency, and a theoretical maximum impulse are identified for a representative nanosatellite-class spacecraft thruster with ideal and nonideal detonation combustion operation using an annular combustor with a plug nozzle and compared to deflagration operation using a traditional converging-diverging nozzle. The volume savings from stored liquid water propellant are also quantified compared to compressed gas tanks with equivalent thruster performance, with some configurations representing a volume reduction of multiple orders of magnitude. recent_works.abstract: An unsteady heat transfer model is proposed for quantifying heat flux and wall temperature profiles in a rotating detonation combustion environment. This work investigates the heat flux trends in rotating detonation combustors to provide higher accuracy than traditional rocket correlations and developed via first principles. It is demonstrated that a one-dimensional analysis is appropriate for describing the effective heat flux and wall temperature profile; this is due to the disparity in length and time scales between thermal diffusion and the wave arrival.
